verified_loci: Wordsworth to Lady Beaumont (1807), Coleridge's remark — 'every great and original writer, in proportion as he is great or original, must himself create the taste by which he is to be relished'
Wordsworth, Essay, Supplementary to the Preface (1815) — 'has had the task of _creating_ the taste by which he is to be enjoyed'
Keats to George and Georgiana Keats (October 1818) — 'I think I shall be among the English Poets after my death.'
Shelley, A Defence of Poetry (1821) — 'the mirrors of the gigantic shadows which futurity casts upon the present'
Stendhal, La Chartreuse de Parme, the last line — 'TO THE HAPPY FEW'
why_seated: Stratum VII, the posterity Bennett's Romantic Poets and the Culture of Posterity (1999) reads as a poetics: the writer who 'must himself create the taste by which he is to be relished' (Wordsworth's letter of 1807, giving it as Coleridge's remark; the Essay of 1815 has 'the task of creating the taste by which he is to be enjoyed'), 'among the English Poets after my death', poets as 'mirrors of the gigantic shadows which futurity casts upon the present', and the novel dedicated at its last line 'TO THE HAPPY FEW'. Nietzsche's 'Einige werden posthum geboren' is seated at EA-CORPORA-27/03 (nietzsche, text/ecce-homo-pg.txt).
ruling: Lee Sharks, 2026-11-07: "i think we need a sappho reception history ea-corpora, whatever's public. translators, scholars. theres some ground work in the archive, notes towards a future reader i believe. the seating can include everything thats publicly available as well as declared absences and pointers for material behind pay- and access- and rights-walls"; and: "sappho reception history + future reader frameworks and related"; and at 12:47 EST, of the first draft: "this seems light on scholarly material related to the future reader proposition or sappho... and that is the focus of notes towards a future reader, is it not?"
